stem: An audit finds three leavers still had active accounts weeks after their last day. Which automation use case addresses this?

options.text: User provisioning and de-provisioning driven by the HR system
options.why: Tying account lifecycle to the authoritative HR record removes the manual step that was missed, in both directions.
Guard rails block a non-compliant action as it is attempted. Nobody attempted anything here; a step simply never happened.

options.text: Automated ticket creation for the service desk
options.why: Closer, and it still depends on a human picking the ticket up. The access is what should be removed automatically.
CI runs checks on code changes. It has no view of employment status.

stem: Engineers keep creating cloud storage that is readable by anyone on the internet. Which automation concept prevents the action rather than reporting it afterwards?

options.why: A guard rail refuses the non-compliant action at the moment it is attempted, so the exposure never exists.
That tells you after the bucket is already public. The stem asks for prevention.
Security groups decide who belongs to what. They do not constrain how a resource is configured.
Raises the work item once the problem exists. Still after the fact.

stem: Which is a genuine drawback of heavily automating security operations?

options.text: The orchestration platform becomes a single point of failure
options.why: When provisioning, access and response all route through one system, its outage or compromise is an outage or compromise of all of them.
Reaction time is one of automation's clearest benefits. It acts in seconds.
Enforcing baselines consistently is exactly what automation is good at.
The objectives list employee retention as a benefit: removing repetitive work keeps people.

stem: A team automates host builds from a single template. A misconfiguration is later found in that template. What does this illustrate?

options.text: Automation multiplies whatever it is given, so one bad baseline reaches every host
options.why: The property that makes automation valuable, perfect consistency at scale, is the same property that scales a mistake.

options.text: Automation is unsuitable for host builds
options.why: Manual builds drift and are worse. The lesson is to review the template, not to stop automating.

options.text: Templates should be replaced by manual configuration
options.why: That trades one consistent error for many inconsistent ones and loses enforceable baselines.

options.text: The misconfiguration proves the automation failed
options.why: The automation did exactly what it was told. The failure is upstream, in what it was told.

stem: A small security team automates triage of low-severity alerts. Which benefit does the exam call this?

options.why: The same number of people cover more ground. The objectives name this explicitly alongside efficiency and reaction time.
Transference moves financial impact to a third party, such as insurance. Nothing moved outside the organisation.
A compensating control substitutes for one you cannot implement. Automation here improves a control you already have.
Layering independent controls is a different idea. This is throughput.

stem: You need to find which internal hosts communicated with a known command and control address over the past six weeks. Which data source is designed for this?

options.why: Flow data records who talked to whom, how much and for how long, and it is small enough to retain for weeks.
Packet capture carries contents and is far too large to hold for six weeks at any scale. You rarely need the payload to answer 'who talked to this address'.
SCAP reports whether a host matches a configuration standard. It sees no traffic.

options.text: SNMP traps from the core switches
options.why: Traps report a device's own state changes, not conversations between hosts.

stem: An auditor asks for evidence that 400 servers match the agreed hardening benchmark. Which tool produces it?

options.text: A SCAP-based configuration scan against the benchmark
options.why: SCAP exists to express a benchmark in machine-readable form and report compliance against it, host by host.
A SIEM correlates events that happened. It does not evaluate a host's current configuration against a standard.
Flow data describes traffic, not configuration.

options.text: A packet capture on the server VLAN
options.why: Traffic contents say nothing about whether a host is hardened.

stem: Analysts receive 600 alerts a day, almost all benign, and have started closing them in bulk without reading. What is the correct response?

options.text: Alert tuning: raise thresholds and suppress known-good patterns
options.why: This is alert fatigue, and the cure is fewer, better alerts. An alert nobody reads provides no detection at all.

options.text: Add more detection rules to improve coverage
options.why: More alerts into a queue nobody reads makes the real one less likely to be seen, not more.
Quarantine is a containment action against one confirmed threat. There is no confirmed threat here, there is noise.

options.text: Discipline the analysts for closing alerts unread
options.why: The behaviour is a rational response to an unworkable queue. The finding is the queue.

stem: An endpoint tool confirms a malicious executable on a laptop. Which activity does the objectives list call this response?

options.why: Isolating the confirmed malicious object or host is the named alert response action, and it buys time to investigate.
Tuning adjusts which alerts fire. This alert was correct and needs acting on.
Aggregation brings logs together so they can be correlated. It is not a response to a confirmed detection.
Archiving retains data for later. It does nothing about the live file.

stem: A fleet includes appliances where no software may be installed. Which monitoring approach fits, and what is the trade?

options.text: Agentless, which needs no install but sees less and depends on reachable credentials or protocols
options.why: Agentless collection works where you cannot deploy software, at the cost of depth and of needing network access and credentials.

options.text: Agent based, because it gives richer data
options.why: Richer, and the scenario says no software may be installed, which rules it out.
Agentless collection exists precisely for this case.

options.text: Install agents anyway and accept the support risk
options.why: On a vendor appliance this usually voids support and may be technically impossible.

stem: A vulnerability programme repeatedly misses hosts. Investigation finds devices in service that appear in no asset register. What is the root problem?

options.text: Asset inventory and tracking: you cannot scan or patch what you do not know exists
options.why: Asset management sits underneath vulnerability management. An incomplete inventory caps how good scanning can ever be.
The scanner covered what it was told about. The gap is what it was never told about.
Cadence governs how fast known hosts are patched. These hosts are not known.
Segmentation limits movement. It neither finds nor registers unknown devices.

stem: Laptops coming off a three year lease must be returned to the leasing company. What is the correct disposal control?

options.text: Sanitization, with a certificate recording that it was done
options.why: The devices are being reused by someone else, so they must be wiped rather than destroyed, and the certificate is the evidence an auditor will ask for.
Destroying drives in leased equipment you must return intact is both a contract problem and unnecessary.

options.text: Deleting the user profiles and reformatting
options.why: Formatting leaves data recoverable. It is not a sanitization method.
Degaussing destroys magnetic media and does nothing to an SSD, which stores no magnetic domains. It also destroys the drive you must return.

stem: A dispute arises over whether a dataset may be shared with a partner, and nobody can say who decides. Which asset management practice was missing?

options.text: Assignment of ownership, with a classification attached
options.why: Every asset needs a named owner who is accountable for classification and access decisions. Without one, questions like this have no answer.

options.text: Enumeration of the asset in the inventory
options.why: Knowing it exists is necessary and does not say who decides about it.
Retention governs how long it is kept, not who may share it.
Disposal is the end of the lifecycle and is not in play.

stem: At which point in the asset lifecycle should security requirements first be applied?

options.text: Acquisition and procurement, before the purchase is made
options.why: Requirements set before buying prevent acquiring something that can never meet policy. Afterwards you are negotiating with a contract already signed.

options.text: At deployment, once the device is on the network
options.why: By then you own something that may be incapable of meeting the standard.
Far too late, and scanning only reports what is already true.
That is the end of the lifecycle.

stem: A requirement states that no unapproved software may execute, including software the company has never seen before. Which control meets it?

options.why: Only permitted software runs, so anything unknown is blocked by default. This is the same logic as a firewall's implicit deny.

options.text: An application deny list of known-bad software
options.why: A deny list permits anything it has no entry for, so it cannot make a promise about software nobody has seen.

options.text: Signature based antivirus with current definitions
options.why: Also an enumerate-the-bad approach. No definition exists for the unseen.
That governs network connections, not which binaries may execute.

stem: A server is fully patched. Which hardening steps still reduce its attack surface?

options.text: Removing unnecessary software, disabling unused services and changing default credentials
options.why: Patching fixes known flaws in what you run. Hardening reduces what you run and what it exposes, including tomorrow's flaw in software you did not need.

options.text: None; a fully patched host is hardened by definition
options.why: A fully patched host with default credentials and every service enabled is still trivially compromised. No patch fixes a default password.
Monitoring detects. It removes no attack surface.
More of the thing already done, and it still does not touch unnecessary services or default credentials.

stem: Which hardening measure blocks malicious behaviour on the host itself rather than filtering its network connections?

options.text: A host based intrusion prevention system
options.why: HIPS watches activity on the host and blocks behaviour it judges malicious, which is a different layer from connection filtering.
That is exactly the network connection filtering the question excludes.
Also a network exposure measure, and a static one.
Segmentation happens between hosts, not on one.

stem: An internet-facing server runs an application the vendor stopped supporting two years ago and the business no longer uses. What is the appropriate mitigation?

options.why: Unused and unsupportable. Removing it eliminates the exposure entirely, which no control applied to a live host can match.

options.text: Isolate it on its own segment and monitor it
options.why: The right answer when the business still needs the system. It does not, so compensating controls are unnecessary cost and residual risk.
There are none; support ended two years ago.

options.text: Add a web application firewall in front of it
options.why: A compensating control for something you must keep running. You do not have to keep this running.

stem: A failed SSD held regulated data and cannot be wiped because it no longer responds. What is the correct disposal route?

options.text: Physical destruction, with a certificate of destruction
options.why: Sanitization requires a working device. When the media has failed, destruction is the only route that guarantees the data is gone, and the certificate is the evidence.
Degaussing erases magnetic domains. An SSD stores charge in flash cells and is completely unaffected by it.
Overwriting is a sanitization method and it needs a drive that responds to writes. This one does not.

options.text: Returning it to the vendor under warranty without further action
options.why: That hands regulated data to a third party. Warranty returns of storage holding sensitive data normally need a destruction clause or a retain-the-drive agreement.

stem: Which statement correctly contrasts an application allow list with a deny list?

options.text: An allow list enumerates what may run and blocks everything else; a deny list enumerates what may not and permits everything else
options.why: The default is what separates them, and it is why only the allow list can make a promise about software nobody has catalogued.

options.text: They are equivalent, differing only in how the list is written
options.why: They have opposite defaults. One fails closed on the unknown, the other fails open.

options.text: A deny list is stronger because it names the actual threats
options.why: Naming threats means the list is only ever as current as the last update, and the set of bad software is unbounded.

options.text: An allow list requires less ongoing maintenance than a deny list
options.why: Reversed. An allow list costs more up front and stabilises; a deny list needs endless updating and is always behind.
